title: Stairmageddon

jokes.text: Stanley struggling to climb the stairs while Dwight named the elevator outage 'Stairmageddon' and ran a weeks-long awareness campaign
jokes.setup: The elevator is down for routine maintenance — a minor workplace inconvenience.
jokes.punchline: Dwight treated it as an apocalyptic event requiring a formal preparedness campaign called 'Stairmageddon,' weeks in advance.
jokes.explanation: This joke works on two levels simultaneously: Dwight's pathological over-preparation for mundane events is deeply character-specific, and it pays off immediately in the physical comedy of Stanley barely surviving a staircase. The name 'Stairmageddon' is a perfectly calibrated piece of Dwight-ism — portentous, bureaucratic, absurd.

jokes.text: Stanley: 'I put 17 damn years into this company, and now they're making me climb stair mountain!'
jokes.setup: Stanley is struggling to walk up one flight of stairs.
jokes.punchline: He frames it as a profound injustice — 17 years of service rewarded with 'stair mountain' — treating a staircase as a personal betrayal.
jokes.explanation: This is a classic Stanley line — the indignant invocation of seniority to justify complete physical laziness. 'Stair mountain' is a perfect coinage: it's how a profoundly sedentary person genuinely experiences one flight of stairs. The 17 years of service as moral currency is hilarious and deeply character-specific. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Talking head: 'Our office has an unusually large number of unusually large people.'
jokes.setup: Multiple employees are visibly struggling to climb the stairs.
jokes.punchline: Dwight delivers the diplomatic double-euphemism 'unusually large number of unusually large people' with complete bureaucratic sincerity.
jokes.explanation: The repetition of 'unusually' is a beautifully economic piece of writing. Dwight almost achieves diplomatic sensitivity but the doubled construction reveals he's just being clinically literal. Perfectly Dwight — he's not trying to be cruel, he's trying to be precise, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head: comparing routine elevator maintenance to 'the end of time' while the camera shows Stanley barely surviving stairs
jokes.setup: Dwight has been deadly serious about Stairmageddon.
jokes.punchline: He pivots to mock others for overreacting — with zero self-awareness that he literally named it an '-armageddon.'
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony is strong — Dwight scorns employees for treating maintenance like the apocalypse while having created an apocalypse-themed campaign. His complete lack of self-awareness is the engine of much Office comedy and it runs cleanly here.

jokes.text: Red alert! Red alert! The reviews are in!
jokes.setup: Andy gets a text about a newspaper review of the documentary.
jokes.punchline: He immediately triggers a 'Red Alert' — the same emergency designation already in use for Stairmageddon — by screaming in the office.
jokes.explanation: Andy's performative panic is consistent with his character's ego-driven anxiety. Works as a solid scene-opener.

jokes.text: Phyllis: 'What does it say?' / Andy: 'I don't know, Phyllis. I just got the text and started screaming Red alert.'
jokes.setup: Andy announces the reviews are in with maximum urgency.
jokes.punchline: He doesn't actually know what they say — he just started yelling before reading.
jokes.explanation: A tight, well-structured beat. Andy's impulsive announcement of something he knows nothing about is both character-specific and structurally clean — the setup is his panic, the punchline is his ignorance. The deadpan delivery implied here makes it land.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'Well, the alert was already set to red because of Stairmageddon. You think I should set it to double red?'
jokes.setup: Andy declares Red Alert for the documentary review.
jokes.punchline: Dwight reveals there is already an existing Red Alert in effect (for Stairmageddon), and earnestly proposes escalating to 'double red.'
jokes.explanation: 'Double red' is the perfect Dwight escalation — he has a formal alert system, it's already maxed out, and his solution is not to question the system but to invent a new tier. The callback to Stairmageddon enriches it. Deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: Review reads: 'Dwight Schrute, the head salesman forever chasing a manager position he will never get.'
jokes.setup: The newspaper review describes each character to the audience.
jokes.punchline: Dwight is summarized with brutal accuracy — 'a position he will never get' — which is both funny and painful given how much of the series this defines.
jokes.explanation: The review is cruel in the way only truth can be. 'Forever chasing a manager position he will never get' is both a perfect character description and a dark joke — particularly resonant for long-time viewers who know how much Dwight has wanted this. Dwight's response ('What does Josh McAuliffe know about the paper business? He works for a news... thing.') adds an extra beat.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'What does Josh McAuliffe know about the paper business? He works for a news... thing.'
jokes.setup: Dwight tries to dismiss a newspaper reviewer's criticism.
jokes.punchline: He can't even name the reviewer's profession — he trails off into 'thing' — undermining his own indignant defense.
jokes.explanation: The trailing 'thing' is the joke — Dwight's contempt for the media collapses into an inability to identify what media even is. Maximum economy: one word does all the work. The momentary pause before 'thing' is where the laugh lives.

jokes.text: Review: 'Andy Bernard, the rudderless trust fund child-slash-middle manager, whose incompetence is emblematic of a declining American economy.'
jokes.setup: The reviewer is describing the documentary subjects.
jokes.punchline: Andy's incompetence is elevated to a symbol of national economic decline — comically outsized meaning for a regional paper manager.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional writing: 'trust fund child-slash-middle manager' is a precise and devastating hyphenation, and connecting one mediocre regional manager's incompetence to the 'declining American economy' is a perfect satirical escalation. It works as character comedy, social satire, and a sharp structural joke all at once. Andy's wounded-but-grateful reaction ('Ouch. Sorry, Andy... It's okay. The hell does he know?') compounds it.

jokes.text: Andy talking head: 'I wanted to be my generation's Lisa Loeb.'
jokes.setup: Andy reflects on the documentary coming out and his future.
jokes.punchline: His dream — framed as a generational artistic aspiration — is to be Lisa Loeb, an extremely niche 90s folk-pop artist.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Lisa Loeb' is what makes this great. Not a rock icon, not a pop star — Lisa Loeb. It reveals Andy's entirely earnest but completely miscalibrated sense of cultural aspiration. 'My generation's Lisa Loeb' also implies that previous generations had their own Lisa Loeb, which opens a comedic rabbit hole. Short, strange, perfect.

jokes.text: Review: 'A lurid subplot reveals the hypocrisy of a local public figure embroiled in a gay affair while preaching family values.' Office reacts: 'Which public figure?'
jokes.setup: The review teases a salacious subplot about a local public figure's hypocrisy.
jokes.punchline: The office collectively plays dumb — Angela, who is married to the Senator, is presumably in the room as everyone speculates.
jokes.explanation: Works as suspense-building dramatic irony for long-time viewers who know about the Senator subplot. The tension between what the audience knows and what the characters pretend not to know is well-constructed here.

jokes.text: Kevin: 'I bet it's Katie Couric. I've been saying this for years.'
jokes.setup: The office speculates about which public figure is 'embroiled in a gay affair.'
jokes.punchline: Kevin confidently names Katie Couric as his long-standing suspect, for no discernible reason.
jokes.explanation: The humor is entirely in Kevin's specificity and conviction. 'I've been saying this for years' implies Kevin has been maintaining this private theory about Katie Couric for years with zero supporting evidence. Classic Kevin — wrong, confident, specific.

jokes.text: Stanley to Dwight: 'Who do I look like, Jackie Joyner-Kersee?'
jokes.setup: Dwight tells Stanley they need to go out on a sales call and implies he should take the stairs.
jokes.punchline: Stanley invokes Olympic track-and-field champion Jackie Joyner-Kersee as the only possible human who could navigate stairs under these conditions.
jokes.explanation: The joke lives entirely in the specificity: not just 'an athlete,' not even just 'an Olympian,' but Jackie Joyner-Kersee specifically. This is deeply Stanley — the kind of person who has a mental catalog of athletic achievements against which he measures his own profound inactivity. It's also absurdist in that Jackie Joyner-Kersee would be unnecessary for one flight of stairs. Highly quotable and character-perfect.

jokes.text: Stanley: 'You are not my damn boss and you never will be!' / Dwight's reaction beat
jokes.setup: Dwight is trying to order Stanley to go on a sales call.
jokes.punchline: Stanley detonates on Dwight with the brutal truth — Dwight is not the manager and never will be — which cuts deeper than Stanley probably intends given the newspaper review.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the newspaper review makes this resonate more than the line alone would. The 'never will be' echoes the review's 'will never get' — a dark through-line. Solid character comedy, though the confrontation itself is less inventive than the surrounding jokes.

jokes.text: Pete being asked for iced tea: 'Three sugars, five creams.' / Pete responding cheerfully: 'Coming right up.'
jokes.setup: In the midst of the chaos, Stanley gives Pete an extremely specific beverage order.
jokes.punchline: Five creams. The absurd ratio reveals Stanley's dietary preferences as an extension of his character.
jokes.explanation: A small but well-placed detail. Five creams is the right number — three would be too reasonable, seven too much. Pete's cheerful compliance adds to the joke. Efficient background comedy.

jokes.text: Pam's Embassy Suites misdirection: she says 'Embassy Suites, do not disturb sign, mommy and daddy on the floor' — then reveals it's marriage counseling
jokes.setup: Coworker asks what Pam and Jim are up to that night; Pam describes what sounds like a romantic getaway with sexual innuendo.
jokes.punchline: It's marriage counseling — the opposite of a passionate evening, recontextualized as a desperate intervention.
jokes.explanation: Clean misdirection structure with emotional weight underneath. 'Mommy and daddy are on the floor' is a great line that works on two levels — the sexy implication and then the sad reality that they can't afford a hotel bed because Jim is funding a startup. The reveal adds cringe and pathos in equal measure.

jokes.text: Toby: 'Did you know that is the only kind of counseling I have never had?'
jokes.setup: Jim mentions he and Pam are going to marriage counseling.
jokes.punchline: Toby catalogs his extensive therapy history and notes that couples counseling is the one gap — implying he has had every other kind.
jokes.explanation: This is quintessential Toby — the implication that he has sampled virtually every variety of therapy except the one for couples (because no one will couple with him) is both funny and genuinely sad. 'The only kind I've never had' does enormous work in six words. Perfect character integration.

jokes.text: Jim asks Toby about his divorce — Toby's exaggerated 'Whoa' followed by 'Oh yeah, no, it's okay. I can handle it.'
jokes.setup: Jim delicately says he wants to ask something 'personal' about Toby's divorce.
jokes.punchline: Toby's initial dramatic recoil ('Whoa') followed by immediate forced bravado ('I can handle it') reveals how raw the wound still is — years later.
jokes.explanation: Classic Toby cringe — his visible pain at the mention of his divorce is a well-worn but still effective beat. The recovery attempt ('I can handle it') while clearly not being able to handle it is good character comedy. Doesn't transcend the familiar Toby-is-sad template.

jokes.text: Jim: 'No, no, no, no. We're just starting couples counseling. Uh, which doesn't sound any better.'
jokes.setup: Jim denies being in couples counseling, then immediately corrects himself.
jokes.punchline: He catches himself mid-denial and acknowledges that 'we're just starting' is arguably worse news than 'we're in,' delivered with his trademark self-aware deadpan.
jokes.explanation: Jim's self-correction is the joke — the meta-awareness that 'just starting' implies it's so new the crisis hasn't even been properly addressed yet. Classic Jim talking-head energy: he sees the irony in real time and narrates it. Clean structure.

jokes.text: Kelly (off-screen): 'Kelly called it. 2013.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam's marriage troubles become known to the office.
jokes.punchline: Someone reveals that Kelly had already predicted Jim and Pam's marriage problems and pinpointed the year 2013.
jokes.explanation: Works as a character joke for Kelly (known for caring intensely about celebrity/office gossip and relationships) and as a wry piece of meta-humor about the show's long-time audience who has been watching Jim and Pam since season one. The specificity of '2013' is the right touch.

jokes.text: Jim chasing Clark out: 'Clark, get outta here. My mistake. Yes, it is your mistake. He's lingering. So annoying. I'm gonna kill him.'
jokes.setup: Jim is embarrassed the office now knows about his marriage counseling.
jokes.punchline: Clark lingers awkwardly while Jim escalates from embarrassed to murderous in rapid succession.
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe beat. The escalation from 'get out' to 'I'm gonna kill him' is mildly funny but not particularly inventive. Clark's awkward lingering is implied visual comedy that would land better on screen.

jokes.text: Andy on hold with William Morris Agency: 'I need to speak with your best agent who represents your biggest stars.' Then immediately hangs up after being corrected.
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to get a talent agent while managing the office crisis.
jokes.punchline: His approach to a major talent agency is to demand their top agent for their biggest stars — as a regional paper company manager with a YouTube video — and then abruptly hangs up when misunderstood.
jokes.explanation: Andy's grandiose self-conception colliding with the mundane reality of his situation. The hang-up is funny but the joke is set up better than it's paid off.

jokes.text: Angela's husband (the Senator): 'Correction. Best darn wife.' Angela: 'Sorry. I'm a better wife than that.'
jokes.setup: The Senator and Angela are preparing to face the press about rumors. Angela says she'll be 'the best damn wife there is.'
jokes.punchline: The Senator corrects her profanity, and Angela immediately self-corrects — performing marital propriety while their marriage is a complete fiction being managed as a PR exercise.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the layers: Angela polices her language about being a good wife while engaged in the ultimate performance of a marriage that is entirely performative. 'I'm a better wife than that' is a great button — she's asserting her quality as a wife by correcting her own profanity. Dark irony working well.

jokes.text: Andy counting YouTube views in real time: '251. 252. I can't even keep up!'
jokes.setup: Andy says his banjo promo has 250 views already.
jokes.punchline: He is refreshing the page during the conversation, counting up one view at a time, treating triple-digit views as a viral phenomenon.
jokes.explanation: The joke is perfectly calibrated: 250-252 views being described as impossible to keep up with is a great satirical observation about amateur self-promotion. Andy's breathless excitement makes it land. Character-specific and observationally sharp.

jokes.text: Dwight produces a bull tranquilizer dart gun to compel Stanley to go on the sales call
jokes.setup: Dwight tells Stanley one way or another he's going on this call.
jokes.punchline: He pulls out a dart gun loaded with bull tranquilizer — an escalation from a management dispute to a veterinary intervention.
jokes.explanation: This is a standout physical comedy moment. The escalation from normal workplace coercion to 'bull tranquilizer' is a perfect Dwight solution — extreme, agricultural, surprisingly practical in his mind. Only Dwight would have a dart gun, would think to use it on a coworker, and would consider it a reasonable management tool. Stanley's 'Holy shit. No, you didn't.' before going down is a great reaction. The moment earns its absurdism through character.

jokes.text: Stanley: 'Holy shit. No, you didn't.' — then gets tranquilized mid-insult
jokes.setup: Dwight is pointing a tranquilizer dart gun at Stanley.
jokes.punchline: Stanley begins his incredulous reaction ('No, you didn't—') and gets cut off mid-sentence by the dart.
jokes.explanation: The timing is everything. 'No, you didn't' is cut off precisely at the moment that proves he did. The interrupted outrage is structurally perfect — Stanley's disbelief becomes the setup for his own unconsciousness. The comedic economy here is exceptional: the punchline arrives before the setup can finish. One of the episode's best constructed moments.

jokes.text: Dwight's defense: 'It's all right. Andy approved it.'
jokes.setup: The office is horrified that Dwight just tranquilized a coworker.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's calm reassurance that everything is fine because Andy approved it — as if managerial approval makes bull-tranquilizing a coworker acceptable.
jokes.explanation: Six words of pure comedic gold. The callback to Andy's careless authorization lands perfectly. Dwight's delivery of this as a completely rational institutional explanation is pitch-perfect character comedy. The implication that 'Andy approved it' is a sufficient answer to the horror of watching a coworker get tranquilized encapsulates everything about this workplace.

jokes.text: Coworker: 'Man, he's really in Twinkle Town now.'
jokes.setup: Stanley is unconscious from bull tranquilizer.
jokes.punchline: 'Twinkle Town' as a euphemism for unconsciousness from a tranquilizer dart is an absurdly gentle description of the situation.
jokes.explanation: A nicely observed line — the softness of 'Twinkle Town' against the hard reality of a tranquilized coworker creates the joke. Less character-specific than the surrounding material but works as reaction comedy.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'This dosage was meant for a very small bull, and Stanley's got way more body fat than they do.' / Coworker notes Dwight gave him three shots.
jokes.setup: Concern that the tranquilizer dosage was meant for a large animal.
jokes.punchline: Dwight specifies it was for a 'very small bull' and reassures by noting Stanley's body fat provides additional protection — plus he gave him three shots.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'very small bull' (already an absurd calibration) to three shots is perfect. Dwight's agricultural logic — Stanley's body fat as a safety buffer, the same way cattle breeds have variable fat percentages — is a Dwight-specific way of thinking about human beings. The reveal of three shots is the kicker.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'Got about 45 minutes to get him to the client before he comes to. Grab his feet.'
jokes.setup: Stanley is unconscious. A normal person would call emergency services.
jokes.punchline: Dwight immediately shifts to logistics: 45-minute window, client meeting, grab his feet. The crisis is a project management problem.
jokes.explanation: The pure Dwight-ness of this is what makes it sing. No moral consideration, no medical concern, just a timeline and a logistics problem. 'Got about 45 minutes' is delivered like a contractor assessing a job. 'Grab his feet' is the perfect no-nonsense button. This line is the engine of the next 10 minutes of the episode.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'He's like a manatee.'
jokes.setup: Dwight and Pete are struggling to move Stanley's unconscious body.
jokes.punchline: Dwight compares Stanley to a manatee — a large, slow, aquatic mammal — with complete matter-of-fact sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximum impact. 'Manatee' is the perfect animal — gentle, enormous, slow-moving, aquatic (implying Stanley is impossible to move on land). Only Dwight thinks in these comparisons. The word itself is funny. This is the kind of throwaway line that becomes a fan-quoted moment. Economy score of 10 is justified: no word could be added or removed.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'No wonder my elevator cables are under such strain.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is struggling to move Stanley's immense weight.
jokes.punchline: Dwight connects the struggle to his earlier concern about elevator cable maintenance — Stanley's weight is why the elevator is broken.
jokes.explanation: A beautiful callback that ties the episode's two main comedy threads together. The elevator being broken and Stanley's weight were separate jokes; here they merge into one implication. Dwight thinking about building maintenance while dragging an unconscious coworker is the perfect character touch.

jokes.text: Pete and Dwight casually discussing weekend plans while dragging unconscious Stanley down the hall
jokes.setup: Dwight and Pete are physically hauling an unconscious tranquilized man through a workplace.
jokes.punchline: Pete breaks the silence with 'Any good weekend plans? I might see a movie.' — treating the situation as entirely routine.
jokes.explanation: The comedy of normalizing the completely insane is Office at its best. Two people making small talk about movies while committing what is functionally a crime against a coworker is a perfect juxtaposition. The mundaneness of 'I might see a movie' is the key — it's so specific and so perfectly ordinary.

jokes.text: Pete, on the wheelbarrow plan: 'Well, if I may, you're a natural.' Dwight: 'Thank you. I mean, I've rehearsed it in my head, like, 1,000 times.' Pete: 'That's a little weird.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is attempting to launch Stanley down the stairs in a wheelbarrow.
jokes.punchline: Dwight reveals he has mentally rehearsed this exact scenario — launching an unconscious person down stairs — approximately a thousand times.
jokes.explanation: The revelation that Dwight has a mental library of emergency personnel-transport scenarios — and has run this specific one a thousand times — is both terrifying and completely consistent with who he is. Pete's 'That's a little weird' is the perfect understatement: yes, it is a little weird to rehearse launching people down stairs in your imagination. 'Evel Knievel' as the reference point is a lovely kicker. One of the episode's best lines.

jokes.text: Dwight's plan: 'I'm gonna launch him. I need you to go to the bottom and catch him.' Pete: 'Catch? I can't catch him, he's like 250 pounds.' Dwight: 'You use your hands and just blunt his descent.'
jokes.setup: They're at the top of the stairs with an unconscious Stanley in a wheelbarrow.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's plan is to 'launch' Stanley down 15 feet of stairs and have Pete 'catch' him by 'blunting his descent' — as if this is a reasonable engineering solution.
jokes.explanation: The dialogue exchange is very well written — Pete's increasingly specific objections ('he's 250 pounds,' 'blunt?,' 'the size of my haunches') against Dwight's completely confident engineering speak create a great escalating rhythm. 'Blunt his descent' as the technical term for catching a large unconscious man is particularly funny.

jokes.text: After the failed launch: 'He would have put a hole in your chest same as he put a hole in that wall.'
jokes.setup: Stanley has apparently crashed into a wall during the aborted launch attempt.
jokes.punchline: Dwight delivers a post-launch damage assessment — Stanley put a hole in the wall — and notes Pete would have suffered similar damage, as if this is a useful safety lesson.
jokes.explanation: The visual of Stanley-shaped hole in the wall is wonderful implied physical comedy. Dwight's deadpan medical/engineering assessment of the damage — comparing Pete's chest to drywall — is perfectly delivered. 'Same as he put a hole in that wall' implies Stanley already demonstrated this property.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam's counseling scene intercut: both arguing their sides of the same incidents without hearing each other
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam are explaining their marriage troubles to a counselor (and the camera), alternating between their POVs.
jokes.punchline: Jim: 'If I didn't do certain things without telling Pam, she'd be married to Roy.' Pam: 'I feel like he's always making decisions for the family and I'm left playing catch-up.'
jokes.explanation: More dark comedy than straight laughs, but Jim invoking Roy — his romantic rival from seasons 1-3 — as justification for unilateral decision-making is both genuinely funny and kind of devastating. It's a perfect character moment: Jim thinks he's making a point; the audience recognizes it as a red flag. The intercutting structure makes it work as comedy rather than drama.

jokes.text: Coworkers watching the press conference: 'Ooh, there's Angela. I work with her.' 'I mean, I'm happy Angela's the first one getting famous, but it's a little weird, no? I mean, she can't sing or act, so it's actually kind of insane, if you think about it.'
jokes.setup: Angela appears on TV at her husband's press conference.
jokes.punchline: Kevin's backhanded commentary — genuinely confused about how Angela got famous since she has no discernible talent — is delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Kevin's confusion about fame is consistent with his character and works as gentle mockery of Angela. The 'she can't sing or act' observation is the right kind of Kevin-logic: he's not being mean, he's being genuinely analytical about the fame meritocracy.

jokes.text: Phyllis: 'Her hair looks beautiful.' Kevin: 'Yeah, we get it, Phyllis, she looks like a freakin' movie star!'
jokes.setup: The office is watching Angela on TV.
jokes.punchline: Kevin explodes at Phyllis for complimenting Angela's hair — his frustration with Angela's undeserved glamour boiling over.
jokes.explanation: A nice secondary beat — Kevin's irritation at having to acknowledge Angela looks good is funny. The 'we get it' implies Phyllis has said this multiple times. Works as a quick character moment.

jokes.text: Senator at press conference: 'I am gay.'
jokes.setup: The Senator has called a press conference to address 'rumors about his personal life' and 'settle things once and for all,' with his 'long-suffering wife' beside him.
jokes.punchline: After all the setup language of a denial, he flatly announces he is gay.
jokes.explanation: The structure is perfect: every phrase in the setup points toward denial ('settle once and for all,' 'long-suffering wife can attest') and then the bomb drops. 'I am gay' after that build is a clean, well-executed misdirection punchline. The economy is exceptional — three words end a long-running subplot. High impact because it's been building for multiple seasons.

jokes.text: Reporter: 'Senator, were you always gay, or did your wife turn you gay?'
jokes.setup: The Senator has just announced he is gay at a press conference.
jokes.punchline: The reporter's question implies being married to Angela is so unpleasant it could cause homosexuality — a dark joke at Angela's expense.
jokes.explanation: This is a darkly sharp line. The premise that a wife could 'turn' her husband gay is absurd and the joke knows it — it's using the absurdity to comment on the Senator's cover story while simultaneously throwing shade at Angela. Works on multiple levels. The delivery in a press conference format makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Reporter: 'Question for the senator's beard.'
jokes.setup: The Senator has outed himself; Angela is standing beside him.
jokes.punchline: A reporter addresses a question to 'the senator's beard' — using the slang term for a partner used as cover for a gay person, which literally also describes Angela's husband's facial hair situation (implied).
jokes.explanation: Economical and sharp. 'Beard' as both the LGBT slang term and a literal description is a clean double meaning delivered with perfect concision. It degrades Angela without the reporter needing to be overtly cruel — the word does all the work.

jokes.text: Senator: 'Yo soy homosexual' — Spanish translation for the crowd
jokes.setup: The Senator has announced he is gay in English.
jokes.punchline: He repeats it in Spanish for 'mis amigos latinos' — treating the coming-out announcement as a multilingual public information service.
jokes.explanation: The joke is the politician's instinct to be inclusive even in the most personal of announcements. He's coming out AND working the room. 'Mis amigos latinos' as the setup phrase is funny in its warmth — he's genuinely trying to be a good politician while his marriage collapses.

jokes.text: Senator: 'It wasn't until my marriage to Angela that I realized how... charmless I find the female body.'
jokes.setup: The Senator is explaining his journey to self-acceptance.
jokes.punchline: He cites his marriage to Angela specifically as the data point that clarified his sexuality — 'how charmless I find the female body' — which is a devastating and specific insult to Angela.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best lines. 'Charmless' is the perfect word — not 'unattractive,' not 'unappealing,' but 'charmless,' which is more damning because it implies a complete absence of appeal rather than mere unattractiveness. The pause before 'charmless' and the attribution to Angela specifically make it extraordinarily cruel and funny simultaneously. Toby's reaction line ('Always hurts to hear that one') adds a perfect kicker.

jokes.text: Toby (watching press conference): 'Ooh. Always hurts to hear that one.'
jokes.setup: The Senator has said Angela's body is 'charmless.'
jokes.punchline: Toby reacts as if this is a broadly relatable experience — 'always hurts to hear that one' — implying women have said this to him specifically.
jokes.explanation: Toby's reaction is the perfect button on the Senator's line. 'Always hurts to hear that one' implies: (1) Toby has heard women describe his body as charmless, (2) he's heard it enough times that it's 'always,' (3) he still hurts from it. Extraordinary character integration — this reaction is only possible from Toby. It turns a joke about Angela into a Toby joke without diminishing either. One of the best reaction beats in the episode.

jokes.text: Senator thanks Oscar Martinez — Oscar is also revealed to be with the Senator
jokes.setup: The Senator has come out as gay. The office assumed this was about Angela's husband and his affair.
jokes.punchline: The Senator names Oscar — their coworker — as the person who 'opened his eyes,' revealing Oscar has been sleeping with Angela's husband.
jokes.explanation: A multi-season payoff landing as a comedy bomb. The audience's dawning realization — confirmed by the coworkers' shocked reactions — makes this a high-impact moment. The reveal that it's Oscar, who they see every day, is the perfect escalation.

jokes.text: Kevin: 'Oscar is with the senator too? Yes! And I knew it the whole time.'
jokes.setup: Oscar's relationship with the Senator is revealed.
jokes.punchline: Kevin claims he 'knew it the whole time' despite having not known, celebrated for the wrong reasons.
jokes.explanation: Kevin's retroactive certainty is a nice character beat. His confidence is always unfounded, and here it's especially funny because he clearly didn't know.

jokes.text: Kevin's extended celebration: 'I kept the secret. I kept the secret so good. You didn't know, you didn't know, and you didn't freaking know. But I knew! He knew! Yes! We did it. You did it, Kevin.'
jokes.setup: Kevin claims he knew about Oscar and the Senator.
jokes.punchline: Kevin delivers a prolonged victory speech to himself and others, talking about his secret-keeping as a team achievement, then awards himself the credit.
jokes.explanation: This is a Kevin classic. The escalating self-congratulation, the pointing at people who 'didn't know,' the framing as a team effort ('we did it') followed by immediate personal credit ('you did it, Kevin') is perfect Kevin logic. The third-person self-address at the end is the ideal button. Highly quotable and deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: Senator announces new partner: 'Wesley Silver.' Multiple people: 'Wesley Silver's gay?'
jokes.setup: The Senator has come out, named Oscar as his affair, and now has a third revelation.
jokes.punchline: Wesley Silver — presumably a well-known local figure — is also gay, also with the Senator, revealed in a cascade of escalating disclosures.
jokes.explanation: The third reveal in a cascade maintains momentum. Works as escalation comedy — the audience expects one revelation and gets three. 'Wesley Silver's gay?' is a nice reaction beat.

jokes.text: Phyllis: 'They make a nice couple.'
jokes.setup: The Senator and Wesley Silver are revealed as a couple on TV while Angela stands beside them.
jokes.punchline: Phyllis — oblivious to the devastation Angela is experiencing — generously observes they make a nice couple.
jokes.explanation: The timing of this line is everything — Phyllis's sincere, gentle approval of the Senator's new relationship while Angela's marriage implodes in real time is perfectly oblivious. Works as a character moment and as an ironic counterpoint to the devastation on screen.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'Are you kidding me? The bubble wrap is the only thing that's stopping his suit from getting wrinkled. These meetings are all about presentation.'
jokes.setup: Someone suggests they can't bring Stanley into the client meeting bubble-wrapped.
jokes.punchline: Dwight defends the bubble wrap not on any safety or dignity grounds but on sartorial ones — the bubble wrap is protecting the suit's presentation.
jokes.explanation: This might be the episode's best pure character joke. Dwight's priority hierarchy — presentation first, unconsciousness second, dignity never — is perfectly expressed. 'These meetings are all about presentation' delivered while transporting a tranquilized man is the ideal encapsulation of Dwight's worldview. The bubble wrap becomes a completely reasonable prop in Dwight's logic system.

jokes.text: Pete's reaction: 'That's actually really smart.' / Dwight: 'Thank you. God, if only there was any other use or situation for that kind of knowledge.'
jokes.setup: Pete accidentally validates Dwight's bubble-wrap logic.
jokes.punchline: Dwight thanks him and then laments that his expertise in wrinkle-free unconscious-person transport has no other applications — completely unaware of the irony.
jokes.explanation: Dwight mourning the single-use nature of his unconscious-body-transport expertise is a perfectly absurd Dwight lament. The complete lack of self-awareness about how insane this all is makes the joke land. 'God, if only' is the right register — genuine wistfulness.

jokes.text: Andy's meeting with talent agent Carla Fern: she represents a 'dog, cat, mouse' act
jokes.setup: Andy has gotten through to a talent agent — Carla Fern — who he was told represents actors, writers, and directors.
jokes.punchline: Carla's actual specialty act is a live animal stacking routine: dog, cat, mouse — with a little hat on the mouse.
jokes.explanation: The incongruity between Andy's Hollywood aspirations and the agent he ends up with — who specializes in a stacked-animal circus act — is good situational comedy. The 'little hat' on the mouse is the perfect detail.

jokes.text: Carla: 'It really doesn't make sense to name the mice. They're kind of like cannon fodder, you know?'
jokes.setup: Andy asks what the mouse's name is.
jokes.punchline: Carla explains that mice die too frequently to justify naming — 'cannon fodder' — delivered with the casual pragmatism of someone who has made peace with mouse mortality.
jokes.explanation: 'Cannon fodder' for mice in a performance act is a darkly funny word choice. The detached practicality of it — Carla has genuinely thought through the mouse-naming calculus — is a great character detail that creates a complete absurd world in one line.

jokes.text: Dwight/Pete logistics exchange: 'I'll grab the forelegs, you push his hindquarters.' Pete: 'Just say arms and legs, okay? That's the vernacular I'm comfortable with.' Dwight: 'Hoist his shank on three.' Pete: 'What's a shank?' Dwight: 'It's by the tenderloin.'
jokes.setup: Dwight and Pete are maneuvering Stanley's unconscious body into a car.
jokes.punchline: Dwight insists on using livestock/butchery terminology for Stanley's body parts ('forelegs,' 'hindquarters,' 'shank,' 'tenderloin') while Pete desperately tries to maintain human dignity.
jokes.explanation: This is the comedic high point of the episode. The escalating vocabulary exchange — forelegs to hindquarters to shank to tenderloin — is meticulously constructed, with Pete's increasingly desperate requests for normal human terminology serving as the straight man. Dwight naturally categorizing Stanley's body in butcher's terms is a profound character joke: to Dwight, a human being and a large bovine are essentially the same logistical problem. 'It's by the tenderloin' as a sincere anatomical locator is perfect. This sequence reaches the 8+ anchor threshold.

jokes.text: Dwight tells the helper to 'get in the back' of the car — helper protests, Dwight insists, helper has to sit in the back with unconscious Stanley
jokes.setup: They need to drive Stanley to the meeting. There are limited seats.
jokes.punchline: The helper is demoted to the back seat with the unconscious, tranquilized Stanley — Dwight gets to drive.
jokes.explanation: A solid physical comedy beat. The visual of the helper squeezed in back with a drugged coworker is good. Dwight's authority assertion ('Get in. Damn it.') is in character. Functional but not one of the episode's best.

jokes.text: Dwight telling Pete to 'get in the back' of the car. Pete reluctantly complies.
jokes.setup: The car has three people: Dwight, tranquilized Stanley in the passenger seat, and Pete needs a seat.
jokes.punchline: Despite Pete doing the actual work, Dwight asserts dominance by relegating Pete to the back seat while the unconscious Stanley rides shotgun.
jokes.explanation: The visual joke — unconscious Stanley in the front seat, awake and functional Pete banished to the back — is implied physical comedy. Dwight's hierarchy giving more respect to a tranquilized coworker than a functioning one is consistent with his character.

jokes.text: Driving to client: Stanley semi-conscious says 'Pigeons.' Dwight: 'Oh God, this is bad.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is briefing the semi-conscious Stanley on the sales meeting as they drive.
jokes.punchline: Stanley's only response to the business briefing is 'Pigeons.' — a non-sequitur that reveals the tranquilizer is affecting his cognition.
jokes.explanation: 'Pigeons.' is a one-word comedy masterpiece in context. The tranquilizer has reduced one of the office's sharpest sardonic minds to free-associating birds. Dwight's 'Oh God, this is bad' reaction is the perfect straight-man button. The economy is extraordinary: one word communicates Stanley's entire cognitive state.

jokes.text: Pete: 'Isn't the client, like, best friends with his sister?'
jokes.setup: The plan to have Pete impersonate Stanley is proposed.
jokes.punchline: Pete points out the client is essentially family — making impersonation instantly impossible and the entire plan absurd.
jokes.explanation: A well-timed reality check that demolishes Dwight's plan in one sentence. The comedic value is in how quickly and completely Pete's observation ends the impersonation idea — and Dwight's immediate 'new plan' pivot.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head: 'You, my friend, are going to have to be Stanley Hudson.'
jokes.setup: Stanley is too drugged to participate in the meeting. Dwight considers his options.
jokes.punchline: Dwight turns to his helper with the most absurd contingency plan — the helper must impersonate Stanley Hudson, a specific Black man with a distinctive personality, despite having nothing in common with him.
jokes.explanation: The confidence with which Dwight delivers this plan is what makes it — 'you, my friend, are going to have to be Stanley Hudson' is said with the gravity of a military briefing. The follow-up 'Isn't the client, like, best friends with his sister?' perfectly deflates the plan before it starts.

jokes.text: Dwight's pivot: 'New plan, okay? We get him a cup of coffee and we go back to the old plan.' / 'Upsie-doozie.'
jokes.setup: The impersonation plan has collapsed.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's 'new plan' is to get the unconscious man some coffee and just... do the original plan, as if coffee will reverse the effects of multiple bull tranquilizer doses. He also says 'upsie-doozie' while lifting Stanley.
jokes.explanation: 'Upsie-doozie' while lifting an unconscious man is a perfect tonal incongruity — the cheery baby-talk lifting phrase applied to a 250-pound tranquilized adult. Dwight's confidence in coffee as a tranquilizer antidote is consistent with his bizarre medical beliefs.

jokes.text: Post-counseling: Toby mutters 'Blah blah blah blah.' Jim: 'Well, they deserve each other, then.' Both: 'That they do. That they do.'
jokes.setup: Toby and Jim are debriefing after the marriage counseling conversation.
jokes.punchline: Both men arrive at mutual contempt for the situation — 'they deserve each other' — with Toby's 'blah blah blah' suggesting the counselor said nothing useful, followed by an awkward over-repetition of agreement.
jokes.explanation: The 'that they do' repetition is a mild awkward-comedy beat — two people running out of things to say while agreeing. Works as a scene button but isn't a strong standalone joke.

jokes.text: Dwight to the client (Mrs. Davis): 'He gets carsick really easily' / Stanley saying 'Driving' while semi-conscious
jokes.setup: Stanley is clearly not fully conscious at the client meeting.
jokes.punchline: Dwight covers by claiming car-sickness; Stanley contributes the single word 'Driving' to the conversation.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the car ride pays off here. 'Driving' as Stanley's contribution to the client meeting — his drugged brain still processing the last thing he was aware of — is a good sustained-absurdism beat.

jokes.text: Half-conscious Stanley at the meeting — fixating on the client's baby photos: 'Look at that baby... Benji... He's precious... I've never seen such a beautiful child.'
jokes.setup: Stanley is barely conscious in the client meeting, supposedly there to close a sale.
jokes.punchline: Stanley, in a tranquilizer haze, becomes obsessed with the client's baby photos — showering them with drug-induced warmth and enthusiasm, utterly derailing the meeting.
jokes.explanation: The joke is maximally effective because the tranquilizer has unlocked a warmer, more demonstrative Stanley than anyone has ever seen. The comedy of Stanley Hudson — famous for his grumpiness — becoming a gushing, baby-admiring sweetheart under pharmaceutical influence is perfect character comedy. 'I've never seen such a beautiful child' from Stanley Hudson is a top-10 Office character beat.

jokes.text: Dwight talking head: 'I must say it's the most pleasant I've ever seen Stanley. I think we should consider injecting him with bull tranquilizer on a daily basis.'
jokes.setup: The sales meeting was a success because Stanley was pleasantly delirious.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's conclusion is not remorse about tranquilizing a coworker but a policy recommendation: daily tranquilizer injections for Stanley.
jokes.explanation: The episode's most quotable line. 'I think we should consider injecting him with bull tranquilizer on a daily basis' is the logical conclusion of Dwight's worldview — he has conducted an experiment, gotten positive results, and is recommending institutionalization of the process. The complete absence of ethical consideration makes this darkly hilarious. 'Consider' adds a bureaucratic nicety that makes it funnier. This will be quoted long after the episode airs.

jokes.text: Andy's talent agency meeting: 'My exact age is 28 to 34, so basically just send me out on whatever Jake Gyllenhaal's going out on.'
jokes.setup: The agent asks Andy's age; he's visibly around 40-45.
jokes.punchline: Andy refuses to give an actual age, instead offering a range ('28 to 34') and then benchmarking himself against Jake Gyllenhaal.
jokes.explanation: '28 to 34' as a self-assessed age range for a 40-something man is already funny; 'Jake Gyllenhaal's going out on' is the perfect escalation. Andy has mapped his own career onto a major film star's with complete sincerity. The agent's deadpan 'Gyllenhaal, got it' reply treats this as information she can work with, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Andy tells the talent agent he can 'sing, play the banjo, innit? And if you hadn't noticed, I've got a pretty good British accent.'
jokes.setup: Andy is pitching himself to a talent agent by listing his abilities.
jokes.punchline: His 'British accent' is presented as a serious performance credential — and 'innit' as the demonstration of it.
jokes.explanation: Using 'innit' as the performance sample for a claimed 'pretty good British accent' is perfectly Andy — his self-assessment has no relationship to external reality. The casualness of 'innit' as proof is great.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Send me out on whatever Jake Gyllenhaal's going out on.' / Agent: 'Gyllenhaal, got it.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just said his exact age is 28-34.
jokes.punchline: He specifically names Gyllenhaal — an A-list film star — as his career peer, and the agent writes it down without blinking.
jokes.explanation: 'Gyllenhaal, got it.' — the agent writing down Jake Gyllenhaal as a comp for Andy Bernard is funny in its deadpan acceptance. She's clearly humoring him, which is itself a joke. Efficient.

jokes.text: Agent asks Andy if he'd dress as a birthday clown for kid's parties and let kids throw pies at him. Andy's response: a long pause, then 'Whereas that is not why I have entered show business, I do understand that you have to build credibility. I'm all for it.'
jokes.setup: Andy has come to this agent imagining himself as the next Jake Gyllenhaal.
jokes.punchline: He talks himself into accepting birthday clown duty by reframing pie-taking as 'building credibility' in show business — the complete capitulation of his ego dressed as wisdom.
jokes.explanation: 'Whereas that is not why I have entered show business' is a beautifully formal construction for someone talking their ego down off a ledge in real time. The self-correction arc — from wounded pride to rationalizing capitulation — happens in two sentences and is entirely in character. Andy's need for validation is stronger than his pride, always.

jokes.text: Carla Fern signs Andy as a client — Andy's extended disbelief and celebration: 'Are you being for real right now?' / 'I need this so bad. I really think this is what could fix me.'
jokes.setup: Andy expected rejection.
jokes.punchline: 'I really think this is what could fix me' — Andy accidentally reveals that he views show business as therapy, not career.
jokes.explanation: 'I really think this is what could fix me' is a great unguarded character moment — Andy's fundamental brokenness leaking out through his excitement. It's simultaneously funny and a little sad, which is Andy at his best.

jokes.text: Signing with Carla Fern requires $5,000 up front — 'that includes headshots.' / 'It doesn't include headshots.' / 'Of course not, because that would be insane if it did.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just celebrated being signed by a talent agent.
jokes.punchline: The agency charges $5,000 upfront (a classic vanity/scam agency model) and doesn't even include headshots — which Andy immediately accepts as reasonable.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed beat. The joke works in layers: (1) $5,000 upfront is a scam agency red flag, (2) the initial promise of headshots raises hope, (3) 'it doesn't include headshots' deflates it, (4) Andy's 'of course not, because that would be insane' accepts the rip-off as the reasonable position. Andy's willingness to rationalize exploitation is perfectly character-specific and lands as a dark joke about desperation.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'You earned yourself a nice, fat commission and you didn't even know it.' Stanley: 'Oh. Silly me. Gotta take the stairs.'
jokes.setup: Stanley has come back to full consciousness and learned he closed a major sale.
jokes.punchline: Stanley's only response to closing a huge deal is immediate existential dread about the stairs — connecting back to the episode's opening premise.
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect callback button to the episode's opening. Stanley wakes up, learns he closed a sale, and his immediate priority is the stair problem — bypassing any reaction to being tranquilized, kidnapped, or used as a sales prop. 'Silly me. Gotta take the stairs.' is devastating in its simplicity. The ellipsis before it ('Oh.') is the whole joke. Stanley's hierarchy of concerns is perfectly expressed: stairs > everything else.

jokes.text: 'Still getting a bargain, though.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just been told the $5,000 doesn't include headshots.
jokes.punchline: Andy's self-reassurance — 'still getting a bargain' — reveals he's actively talking himself into an obvious scam.
jokes.explanation: A five-word button that lands cleanly. Andy's self-deception is complete — 'still getting a bargain' while paying $5,000 for nothing. Economy score is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Final scene: Stanley refuses to take the stairs back up. Dwight: 'We need a winch and a hoist.'
jokes.setup: Dwight got Stanley down; now Stanley refuses to take the stairs back up.
jokes.punchline: The episode ends on the same problem it started with — Stanley vs. stairs — escalated to requiring industrial lifting equipment.
jokes.explanation: The episode closes the loop with perfect structural economy. The premise (Stanley won't take stairs) has escalated to its logical absurd conclusion (Stanley won't take stairs ever again and requires a winch). 'We need a winch and a hoist' is a great final line — it implies this problem has no solution, the episode will never be resolved, and Stanley has permanently won. Excellent structural comedy.

tmdb_overview: The elevator goes out at the office, forcing everyone to use the stairs. Dwight forces Stanley to make a sales call. Pam and Jim talk to Nellie and Toby about relationship problems. Angela supports her man.
